Cedric: Invented by Walter Scott for Ivanhoe (1819), probably a misspelling of Cerdic, an Old English/Celtic name of uncertain meaning.
Jeremy: English form of Jeremiah, from Hebrew Yirmeyahu, usually explained as 'Yahweh exalts' or 'Yahweh loosens'.
Cloé: French form of Chloe, from Greek khloe, 'green shoot' or 'young verdure'; an epithet of the goddess Demeter.
Dennis: English form of Denis, from Greek Dionysios, 'follower of Dionysus', the god of wine.
Hendrik: Dutch form of Henry, from Germanic heim 'home' and rik 'ruler': 'home ruler'.
Semih: Turkish, from Arabic Sami' or Samih, meaning 'generous' or 'magnanimous'.
Sandro: Italian short form of Alessandro, the Italian Alexander, from Greek 'defender of men'.
Burak: Turkish, from Arabic Buraq, the winged steed of the Prophet Muhammad's night journey; also linked to 'lightning'.
Sofian: Variant of Sofiane, Arabic Sufyan, from a root meaning 'swift' or 'one who sails smoothly'; a companion's name in early Islam.
Marina: Latin, 'of the sea', feminine of Marinus. Used across Europe and the Slavic world.
Jona: Short form of Jonah or Jonas, from Hebrew Yonah, 'dove'.
Zohra: Arabic Zahra, 'radiant, shining'; Zohra is the North African and Persian form.
Merlijn: Dutch form of Merlin, the wizard of Arthurian legend, from Welsh Myrddin, possibly 'sea fortress'.
Irene: Greek Eirene, 'peace'. Name of the Greek goddess of peace and of an early Christian saint.
Maurits: Dutch form of Maurice, from Latin Mauritius, 'dark-skinned' or 'Moorish', from Maurus.
Jurre: Frisian and Dutch short form of Joris or Jurriaan, ultimately from Greek Georgios, 'farmer'.
Nelly: English pet form of Helen, Eleanor or Cornelia, so meaning depends on the source name.
Carlos: Spanish and Portuguese form of Charles, from Germanic karl, 'free man'.
Félicie: French feminine form of Félix, from Latin felix, 'happy, fortunate'.
Lilas: French for 'lilac', the flower, ultimately from Persian via Arabic lilak, 'bluish'.
Salwa: Arabic, 'solace, comfort'; also the name of a quail-like bird in the Quran.
Helen: English form of Greek Helene, of uncertain meaning, possibly 'torch' or 'shining one'.
Rosy: English and French diminutive of Rose, from the flower name, or an adjective 'rosy'.
Nadine: French, from Russian Nadezhda via Nadia, meaning 'hope'.
Athénaïs: French form of Greek Athenais, 'of Athena', the goddess of wisdom.
Valeria: Latin feminine of Valerius, a Roman family name from valere, 'to be strong, healthy'.
Daryl: English, from the surname Darrell, from French d'Airelle, a Norman place name. Used as a given name since the 20th century.
Noë: French form of Noah, Hebrew Noach, usually explained as 'rest' or 'comfort'. Here given to a girl.
Ioana: Romanian form of Joanna, from Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'.
Lyla: Variant of Layla, Arabic 'night'; also used in English as a modern name.
Kamelia: Variant of Camellia, the flower named after Jesuit botanist Georg Kamel. Also used in Arabic as 'perfect' (Kamila).
Siena: From the Tuscan city of Siena, of uncertain, probably Etruscan or Latin origin. Used as a modern given name.
Yacoub: Arabic form of Jacob, from Hebrew Yaakov, usually explained as 'holds the heel' or 'supplanter'.
Rosaline: Variant of Rosalind or Rosalie, from Germanic 'horse' and 'gentle', influenced by Latin rosa 'rose'.
Ralf: Variant of Ralph, from Old Norse Raðulfr, 'counsel wolf'.
Swa: Probably a short form of a Dutch or Flemish name such as Swa(ntje) or Sylvain; origin uncertain.
Alea: Latin alea, 'dice' (as in 'the die is cast'); also used as a modern coined name. Origin as a given name uncertain.
Tasniem: Arabic Tasnim, the name of a spring in Paradise in the Quran, from a root meaning 'to rise high'.
Suus: Dutch pet form of Susanna, from Hebrew Shoshannah, 'lily'.
Agatha: Latin form of Greek Agathe, from agathos, 'good'. Saint Agatha was a Sicilian martyr.
Puck: English and Dutch, from the mischievous sprite of folklore and Shakespeare, from Old English puca, 'goblin'.
Isadora: Greek, 'gift of Isis', from Isis and doron 'gift'. A feminine form of Isidore.
Rory: Anglicised Irish Ruairí, from Gaelic 'red king'. Also used for girls in modern times.
Romee: Dutch, probably a variant of Romy, a short form of Rosemarie or Romina; origin uncertain.
Layaan: Probably a variant of Arabic layyin or Layan, 'soft, gentle'. Modern name; origin uncertain.
Rapha: Short form of Raphaël, from Hebrew 'God heals'; also Hebrew rapha, 'he healed'.
Arès: French form of Ares, the Greek god of war; origin of the word is uncertain.
Corentin: Breton, from Korentin, a 5th-century saint of Quimper; origin uncertain, possibly 'hurricane' or 'friend'.
Brian: Irish and Celtic, of uncertain meaning, perhaps 'high' or 'noble'. Made famous by Brian Boru.
Laurent: French form of Laurentius, 'from Laurentum', or Latin laurus, 'laurel'.
Anne: French and English form of Hannah, from Hebrew Chanah, 'grace, favour'.
Imke: Frisian and Low German diminutive of names beginning Im- or Irm-, from Germanic irmin, 'whole, great'.
Nico: Short form of Nicolaas or Nicolas, from Greek Nikolaos, 'victory of the people'.
Jozefien: Dutch feminine form of Joseph, from Hebrew Yosef, 'God will add'.
Michel: French and Dutch form of Michael, from Hebrew 'who is like God?'.
Ilian: Probably a variant of Elian or Ilyan, linked to Greek helios 'sun' or Welsh Eilian; origin uncertain.
Hadrien: French form of Hadrian, from Latin Hadrianus, 'from Hadria', a town in northern Italy.
Ilayda: Turkish, probably from Ilayda, a modern name possibly meaning 'a gift from God'; origin uncertain.
Ilhan: Turkish, 'ruler of the realm', from il 'country' and han 'khan'.
Emirhan: Turkish, a compound of Arabic emir 'commander' and Turkic han 'ruler'.
Jay: English, from the bird, or a short form of names beginning with J, such as Jason or James.
Zuzanna: Polish form of Susanna, from Hebrew Shoshannah, 'lily'.
Timeo: Probably from Greek Timaios, 'honoured', or Latin timeo 'I fear'; compare Timothy. Origin uncertain.
Pedro: Spanish and Portuguese form of Peter, from Greek petros, 'rock, stone'.
Mano: Probably a short form of Manolo or Emmanuel, Hebrew 'God is with us'; origin uncertain.
Yaël: French form of Yael, Hebrew for 'ibex' or 'mountain goat'. A biblical heroine; used for both sexes.
Carmen: Spanish, from Carmel, Hebrew 'garden, orchard', influenced by Latin carmen 'song'.
Fie: Flemish and Danish short form of Sophie, from Greek sophia, 'wisdom'.
Babs: English pet form of Barbara, from Greek barbaros, 'foreign'.
Camil: Variant of Camille, from Latin Camillus, a Roman family name of uncertain meaning, perhaps 'attendant at a ritual'.
Camilia: Variant of Camilla, from the Latin family name Camillus; possibly also influenced by the camellia flower.
Lexy: English pet form of Alexandra, from Greek 'defender of men'.
Annie: English diminutive of Anne, from Hebrew Chanah, 'grace, favour'.
Amadéo: Variant of Amadeo, Italian and Spanish, from Latin 'love God'.
Federico: Italian and Spanish form of Frederick, from Germanic 'peaceful ruler'.
Andreea: Romanian feminine form of Andrew, from Greek andreios, 'manly, brave'.
Bayane: Arabic Bayan, 'clarity, eloquence, explanation'. Used as a girl's name in francophone North African families.
Yavuz: Turkish, 'stern, fierce, resolute'; associated with the Ottoman sultan Selim 'the Grim'.
Aurelio: Italian and Spanish, from Latin Aurelius, a Roman family name from aureus, 'golden'.
Imany: Modern name, from Arabic iman, 'faith'; Swahili form also exists. Popularised by a French singer.
Pavel: Slavic form of Paul, from Latin Paulus, 'small, humble'.
Eugène: French form of Eugene, from Greek Eugenios, 'well-born, noble'.
Dea: Latin for 'goddess'; also used in Albanian and Italian as a short form of names such as Andrea or Dea Maria.
Ghita: Short form of Margherita or Margarita, from Greek margarites, 'pearl'. Also Arabic Ghita.
Umar: Arabic, possibly 'flourishing' or 'long-lived'. The second caliph of Islam bore this name.
Aissata: West African form of Aisha, Arabic 'alive, living'.
Amelya: Variant of Amelia, from Germanic amal, 'work', mixed with Latin Aemilia, 'rival'.
Elhadj: From Arabic al-hajj, 'the pilgrim', a title for one who has made the hajj to Mecca.
Mariya: Slavic and Arabic form of Maria, from Hebrew Miriam, of uncertain meaning, possibly 'beloved'.
Micah: Hebrew Mikha, short form of Mikhayahu, 'who is like Yahweh?'. A biblical prophet.
Lando: Short form of Orlando or Landolf, from Germanic 'land' and 'wolf'; also an Italian name.
Kimya: Arabic and Persian, from kimiya, 'alchemy'; also Swahili and Turkish usage. Rare given name.
Eyad: Arabic Iyad, 'support, strength', or from a tribal name.
Marlo: Probably from the surname Marlow, Old English 'remnant of a lake'. Modern given name for both sexes.
Milhan: Probably a modern variant of Mylan or Arabic Milhan; origin uncertain, possibly 'gracious'.
Alpaslan: Turkish, 'heroic lion', from alp 'hero' and arslan 'lion'; name of the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan.
Éva: French and Hungarian form of Eve, from Hebrew Chavah, 'life, living'.
Liham: Origin uncertain; possibly a modern or Arabic-influenced coinage, or a variant of Lyam, a form of William.
Muaz: Arabic Mu'adh, 'protected, sheltered'; a companion of the Prophet Muhammad.
Romie: Probably a variant of Romy, a short form of Rosemarie, or a feminine of Romeo. Origin uncertain.
Husna: Arabic, 'most beautiful, good', from the root of husn, 'beauty'.
Asra: Arabic, 'night journey' or 'one who travels at night'; also Turkish use, and Urdu 'asra' meaning 'support'.
Eddie: English diminutive of Edward or Edgar, from Old English 'wealth guardian'.
Elyanna: Modern blend of Eliana or Elyan and Anna; Eliana is Hebrew 'my God has answered'.
Nahël: Probably a variant of Nahel, Arabic for 'one who drinks, one who quenches thirst'; popular in France.
Anaïa: Probably a modern variant of Anaya or Anaïs; Sanskrit and Hebrew roots are both claimed. Origin uncertain.
Aëlys: Modern French coinage, probably a variant of Alice or Aélis, from Germanic 'noble kind'.
Zeyn: Variant of Zain or Zayn, Arabic 'beauty, grace'.
Sézanne: From the French town of Sézanne in Marne, of Gaulish or Latin origin. Rare as a given name.
Usayd: Arabic Usayd, a diminutive of asad, 'lion'; a companion of the Prophet.
Brent: English, from a surname and place name meaning 'burnt' or from Celtic 'high place'.
Elien: Dutch and Flemish, probably a variant of Eliane or Elina, from Greek Helios 'sun' or Helene 'torch'.
Mathijs: Dutch form of Matthew, from Hebrew Mattityahu, 'gift of God'.
Laly: Probably a pet form of Laura or Eulalie, the latter from Greek 'well-spoken'.
Hayley: English, from a surname and place name meaning 'hay clearing'.
Daphne: Greek, 'laurel'. The nymph who turned into a laurel tree to escape Apollo.
Ina: Short form of names ending in -ina, such as Katrina or Georgina; also Germanic 'one'.
Lode: Flemish short form of Lodewijk (Louis), or of Lodewijk's relative Lodovicus, 'famous in battle'.
Eveline: Norman French diminutive of Eve or from Germanic Avelina, possibly 'hazelnut' or 'desired'.
Alissa: Variant of Alyssa, from Alice, from Germanic Adalheidis, 'noble kind'; also associated with Greek 'sane'.
Méline: French, possibly from Latin Melina 'honey-like' or a form of Mélanie or Emmeline. Origin uncertain.
Ranya: Arabic Rania, 'gazing, looking' or 'queen' in Sanskrit-derived use.
Sverre: Norwegian, from Old Norse Sverrir, probably 'wild, swinging'. Name of a medieval Norwegian king.
Linda: Germanic and Spanish, 'soft, tender' or Spanish 'pretty'; also a short form of names ending in -linda.
Faith: English virtue name, from Latin fides, 'trust, belief'.
Naomie: French variant of Naomi, from Hebrew 'pleasantness'.
Yaëlle: French feminine form of Yael, Hebrew 'ibex, mountain goat'.
Kawthar: Arabic, 'abundance'; a river in Paradise and the title of Sura 108 of the Quran.
Félicien: French, from Latin Felicianus, derived from felix, 'happy, fortunate'.
Fauve: French for 'wild beast' or 'tawny'; a rare given name, in Belgium sometimes used for girls.
Fiene: Flemish, a variant of Fien, a short form of Josephine or Sophie.
Juliana: Latin feminine of Julianus, from the Roman family name Julius, of uncertain meaning, perhaps 'youthful'.
Eléana: Variant of Eleana or Eliana, probably from Greek 'torch' or Hebrew 'my God has answered'.
Abderrahman: Arabic Abd al-Rahman, 'servant of the Merciful', one of the names of God.
Nathéo: Modern French coinage, blending Nathan or Nathaniel ('gift' in Hebrew) with Théo ('God' in Greek).
Romaissa: Arabic, from Rumaysa, a female companion of the Prophet; the meaning is uncertain, possibly 'sweet scent'.
Eleana: Variant of Eliana or Eleanor; Eliana is Hebrew 'my God has answered'; also linked to Greek Helene.
Zélia: Portuguese and French, from Greek zelos, 'zeal', or a form of Zelie. Also found as a form of Celia.
Nelles: Dutch surname-like form, probably from Nelis, a short form of Cornelis, from Latin Cornelius.
Abraham: Hebrew, 'father of many nations' (Avraham), the biblical patriarch.
Romaysa: Variant of Rumaysa, an Arabic name of a companion of the Prophet; meaning uncertain, possibly 'sweet-smelling'.
Vlad: Slavic short form of Vladimir or Vladislav, from Old Slavic 'rule' with 'peace' or 'glory'.
Leonore: German and Dutch form of Eleonore or Leonora, short for Eleanor; origin possibly Provençal Alienor.
Clarice: French and English form of Clarissa, from Latin clarus, 'bright, clear, famous'.
Ebe: Probably a Frisian or Dutch short form of a Germanic name such as Ebbe or Eberhard; origin uncertain.
Keyla: Modern name, a variant of Kayla, possibly from Hebrew 'crown' or Gaelic 'slender'; origin uncertain.
Zaïd: Arabic Zayd, 'growth, abundance'; the adopted son of the Prophet Muhammad.
Louve: French for 'she-wolf'; a rare modern given name.
Maha: Arabic, 'wild cow' or 'oryx', a symbol of beautiful eyes; also Sanskrit 'great'.
Till: German and Dutch short form of Dietrich or Ulrich, as in Till Eulenspiegel.
Sahar: Arabic, 'dawn' or 'the time before sunrise'; also Persian and Hebrew uses.
Rahim: Arabic, 'merciful, compassionate', one of the names of God.
Loann: Breton or French variant of Loan or Yoann, from John, Hebrew 'God is gracious'.
Ayleen: Probably a variant of Eileen or Aylin; Eileen is Irish form of Helen, Aylin is Turkish 'halo around the moon'.
Edin: Bosnian and Balkan, from Arabic and Turkish roots meaning 'Eden' or 'paradise'; also Scottish 'Edin' for Edinburgh.
Bodhi: Sanskrit and Pali, 'awakening, enlightenment'. The tree under which the Buddha attained it.
Conor: Anglicised Irish Conchobhar, 'lover of hounds' or 'high desire'.
Cami: Short form of Camille or Camilla, from the Latin family name Camillus.
Ragnar: Old Norse Ragnarr, 'warrior of the gods' or 'wise army'.
Edis: Probably a variant of Edith or the Turkish Edis; Edith is Old English 'prosperous in war'. Origin uncertain.
Tommaso: Italian form of Thomas, from Aramaic te'oma, 'twin'.
Alphonse: French form of Alfonso, from Germanic 'noble and ready'.
Tylio: Modern coined name, probably from Tyler or Tilio, a variant of Emilio. Origin uncertain.
Vidar: Old Norse Víðarr, a god of vengeance; probably 'wide warrior' or 'forest warrior'.
Ozanne: French, possibly from Hosanna or the Germanic name Osanne; origin uncertain. Rare feminine name.
Zayne: Variant of Zane or Zayn, from Arabic 'beauty, grace', or English Zane, a form of John.
Achim: German short form of Joachim, from Hebrew 'Yahweh establishes'.
Jessica: Invented by Shakespeare for The Merchant of Venice, probably from Hebrew Yiskah, 'he beholds'.
Myrthe: Dutch form of Myrtle, from Greek myrtos, the evergreen myrtle plant, symbol of love.
Joris: Dutch form of George, from Greek Georgios, 'farmer'.
Thibeau: Variant of Thibault or Thibaut, from Germanic theud 'people' and bald 'bold'.
Laurien: Dutch, a form of Laura or Laurentia, from Latin laurus, 'laurel'.
Tamara: Hebrew Tamar, 'date palm'; widely used in Georgia and Russia, after Queen Tamar.
Dylano: Modern extension of Dylan, Welsh 'son of the sea', with an Italianate ending.
Phoebe: Greek Phoibe, 'bright, radiant'; a Titan and a title of Artemis.
Amanda: Latin, 'worthy of love'. First recorded in 17th-century English literature.
Menno: Frisian short form of Germanic names with magin or megin, 'strength'. Menno Simons founded the Mennonites.
Audric: Norman French, from Germanic Aldric or Audric, 'old ruler' or 'noble ruler'.
Johannes: Latin and Germanic form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'.
Gatien: French, from Latin Gratianus, 'grace'; Saint Gatien was the first bishop of Tours.
Loukas: Greek form of Luke, from Latin Lucas, 'man from Lucania' or 'light'.
Nihal: Turkish and Arabic, 'young plant, sapling' (from Persian); also Sanskrit and Hindi 'content'.
Tenzin: Tibetan, 'holder of the teachings' (Buddhist doctrine), as in the Dalai Lama's name.
Moshe: Hebrew form of Moses, from Egyptian 'born' or Hebrew 'drawn out' (of water).
Ennio: Italian, from the Roman family name Ennius, of uncertain origin. Ennius was an early Roman poet.
Joel: Hebrew Yoel, 'Yahweh is God'. A minor biblical prophet.
Armin: German form of Arminius, the Germanic leader Hermann, probably from Latin or Germanic 'whole, army man'.
Mélia: Probably a short form of Amélie or Mélanie, or from Greek melia, 'ash tree'. Origin uncertain.
Gaspar: Spanish, Portuguese and French form of Caspar, one of the Three Kings; possibly Persian 'treasurer'.
